name: Papaya
short: Ripe papaya, in small amounts, is usually fine. Raw or unripe papaya is the kind to skip.
why: Fully ripe papaya is a nourishing fruit. Unripe or semi-ripe papaya has more latex (papain), which is traditionally avoided in pregnancy. The riper it is, the gentler it is.
t1: Many women like to be extra careful in the first trimester and skip raw papaya completely.
indian: Raw papaya turns up in salads and some sabzis, and that's the form to be careful with. Ripe, sweet papaya as a fruit is the safer choice.

name: Pineapple
short: Pineapple in normal amounts is fine. Only very large quantities are best avoided.
why: Pineapple has an enzyme called bromelain, but a normal serving holds very little. You'd have to eat a lot for it to matter, so everyday portions are fine.
t1: Nausea may put you off it anyway. A few slices of ripe pineapple are fine. The fear that it starts labour is a myth at any amount you'd eat.
t3: Still a myth: no plate of pineapple brings on labour. Heartburn from its acidity is the more likely trouble now.
indian: A few slices or a glass of fresh juice is fine. Skip the big bowl every day.

name: Mango
short: Yes, in moderation. Mango is a nourishing fruit.
why: Mango is rich in vitamins A and C and folate. It's also high in natural sugar, so keep portions sensible, especially if your doctor is watching your blood sugar.
t1: A good fruit if you can keep it down. Go easy on very ripe, very sweet ones if sugar makes you feel sick.
t2: Enjoy the season. If a glucose test is due, a mango a day adds a lot of sugar to that result.
t3: If you've been told to watch your sugars (gestational diabetes), this is the fruit to count.
indian: Wash well and enjoy it in season. If you have gestational diabetes, or are at risk of it, ask your doctor how much is right for you.

name: Banana
short: Yes. Bananas are an easy, filling pregnancy snack.
why: They give quick energy and potassium, can settle early nausea and help with constipation. A simple, reliable choice.

name: Paneer
short: Paneer made from pasteurised milk, eaten fresh or cooked, is fine. Skip unpasteurised soft cheese.
why: The worry with some soft cheeses is listeria, a germ that can grow in unpasteurised dairy. Paneer from pasteurised milk, cooked or freshly made, avoids that.
indian: Branded paneer and most home-made paneer use pasteurised milk. If you're not sure, cook it (paneer bhurji, palak paneer) instead of eating it raw.

name: Curd / Yoghurt
short: Yes. Curd is safe and good for you in pregnancy.
why: Made from pasteurised milk, it gives you calcium and protein, and its probiotics can help digestion. Set curd at home or buy packaged dahi.

name: Chocolate
short: Yes, in moderation. Chocolate is fine to enjoy.
why: Chocolate has a little caffeine, so it counts towards your daily caffeine total. A few squares are a nice treat. Keep the overall amount sensible.

name: Street Food
short: It depends on hygiene and freshness. The risk is contamination, not the dish itself.
why: Pregnancy lowers your defence against food infections. Hot food, freshly cooked at a busy, clean stall, is far safer than anything left out, raw, or rinsed in tap water.
t1: Nausea often decides for you. If you do eat out, choose hot, freshly fried food from a stall you trust.
t2: Freshly cooked and hot, from a busy stall. Skip chutneys, cut fruit and pani that have been sitting out.
t3: Same rules. A stomach infection in the last weeks can bring on early labour.
indian: The usual culprits are golgappa or pani puri water, cut fruit, and chutneys made with unfiltered water. Piping-hot tikki or dosa, freshly made, is lower risk.

name: Honey
short: Yes. Honey is fine for you in pregnancy.
why: The well-known honey warning is for babies under one year, not for you. An adult's gut handles honey normally. It's still sugar, so keep an eye on the amount.

name: Ginger
short: Yes. Ginger in food and tea is fine, and it can ease nausea.
why: Ginger is one of the better-studied natural remedies for morning sickness. The amounts used in cooking and tea are considered safe. You don't need large supplement doses.
t1: This is when it helps most. Ginger tea, ginger candy or a little fresh ginger settles nausea for many women.
t2: Fine in cooking and chai. You don't need very large amounts, like supplements.
t3: Fine in food. It can make heartburn worse, so go by how you feel.
indian: Adrak in your chai, or a little ginger and honey in warm water, is a gentle, traditional way to settle queasiness.

name: Coffee
short: Up to about one cup a day (under about 200mg caffeine) is generally fine.
why: The usual advice is to keep your total caffeine under roughly 200mg a day. It adds up across coffee, tea, cola and chocolate, not coffee alone.
t1: Many women go off coffee in the first trimester. If you do, go with it.
t2: One cup a day is the usual limit. Tea, cola and chocolate count towards it.
t3: Caffeine late in the day can cost you sleep that's already hard to get. Keep it to the morning.
indian: A strong South Indian filter coffee can have more caffeine than you'd think. One a day is a sensible limit.

name: Tea / Chai
short: Yes, in moderation. Regular tea is fine. Keep an eye on your total caffeine.
why: Tea has less caffeine than coffee, but it still counts towards your roughly 200mg daily limit. Two to three cups of normal chai is generally fine.
t1: Ginger chai helps some women with nausea. Two cups a day is a sensible limit, counting any coffee.
t2: Two cups a day, and not with your iron tablet. Tea blocks iron absorption for about an hour.
t3: The same two cups, earlier in the day. It's kinder to your heartburn and your sleep.
indian: Doodh wali chai counts too. Some herbal teas aren't recommended in pregnancy, so check before you switch to a new one.

name: Green Tea
short: One to two cups a day is usually fine. Just don't overdo it.
why: Green tea has caffeine, and in large amounts it can get in the way of how your body uses folate, which matters early in pregnancy. A cup or two is fine. Many cups a day is not.
t1: It counts towards your daily caffeine. Have one cup, and not with your folic acid, as green tea can lower how much you absorb.

name: Coconut Water
short: Yes. Coconut water is a great way to stay hydrated.
why: It's mostly water with natural electrolytes, so it keeps you hydrated and can soothe a queasy stomach. Fresh is best.
t1: A gentle drink when nausea makes water hard to get down. Sip it through the day.
t3: Good for swelling and cramps. It's a natural source of potassium.
indian: Nariyal paani is widely recommended. Drink it fresh from a tender coconut, not a sugary packaged one.

name: Buttermilk
short: Yes. Buttermilk is safe, cooling and good for digestion.
why: Made from curd, it gives you calcium and probiotics, helps with acidity and keeps you hydrated. It's light and easy on the stomach.
indian: Chaas with a little jeera and pudina is a lovely everyday drink, especially in summer.

name: Alcohol
short: No. No amount of alcohol is considered safe in pregnancy.
why: Alcohol crosses the placenta to your baby, and no safe amount or safe time has been found. The clear advice is to avoid it completely. Many women have a drink before they know they're pregnant. That's rarely a problem. Stop now, and tell your doctor at your next visit.
t1: No safe amount, and the first trimester is when your baby is most vulnerable. A drink before you knew is rarely a problem: stop now and tell your doctor.
t2: No safe amount.
t3: No safe amount.

name: Soft Drinks / Soda
short: One now and then is okay, but they're high in sugar and caffeine.
why: Colas add caffeine to your daily total, and most soft drinks are very sugary with little benefit. Fine as an occasional treat, not as an everyday drink.
t2: Cola counts towards caffeine. The sugar matters more as your glucose test gets closer.
t3: If you have gestational diabetes, a regular cola is off the list.

name: Water (how much)
short: Yes, drink plenty. Staying well hydrated is one of the easiest good habits.
why: Aim for roughly 8 to 10 glasses a day, more in the heat or if you're active. Good hydration helps with constipation, swelling and those common Braxton Hicks tightenings.

name: Paracetamol (Crocin / Dolo)
short: Paracetamol is usually the first choice for fever or pain in pregnancy. Take the lowest dose that helps, for the shortest time.
why: It's the most widely used pain and fever medicine in pregnancy and is usually preferred over the others. Still, take it only when you need it, and tell your doctor if you're taking it often.
t1: The one painkiller considered safe at every stage. Take the usual dose for the shortest time. A fever is a reason to call your doctor, not only to treat it.
t2: Same: the usual dose, for the shortest time.
t3: Same. If you need it every day for headaches, tell your doctor. Headaches with swelling need checking.

name: Ibuprofen
short: Usually avoided in pregnancy, especially in the third trimester. Ask your doctor first.
why: Ibuprofen is an anti-inflammatory (NSAID) that's usually not recommended in pregnancy, especially later on. Paracetamol is normally suggested instead.
t1: Avoid it. There's a small link to miscarriage in early pregnancy. Take paracetamol instead.
t2: Avoid it unless your doctor prescribes it for a specific reason.
t3: In the third trimester it's best avoided completely, because it can affect the baby. Don't take it without your doctor.

name: Combiflam
short: Best not taken on your own, because it contains ibuprofen. Check with your doctor.
why: Combiflam mixes paracetamol with ibuprofen, and ibuprofen is the part usually avoided in pregnancy. For fever or pain, plain paracetamol is the safer first choice.
t1: Avoid it: it contains ibuprofen. Take plain paracetamol instead.
t2: Avoid it unless it's prescribed.
t3: Avoid it completely. The ibuprofen in it is unsafe after 30 weeks.

name: Antibiotics
short: Some are safe in pregnancy and some aren't. Take only the antibiotics your doctor prescribes.
why: It depends on which antibiotic. Several are used safely in pregnancy and a few are avoided. Never choose one yourself, and never reuse an old strip from the cupboard.

name: Folic Acid
short: Yes. Folic acid is recommended in pregnancy. Take it the way your doctor advises.
why: It helps your baby's brain and spine form early on, which is why it's advised from before conception through early pregnancy. It's one of the few things you're actively encouraged to take.
t1: It matters most in the first trimester, and ideally before. Please don't skip it.
t2: Keep taking it. Most pregnancy tablets include it.
t3: Keep taking it as part of your pregnancy tablet. There's no reason to stop.

name: Iron Supplements
short: Yes. Iron is commonly recommended. Take the dose your doctor prescribes.
why: Your blood volume rises in pregnancy, so you need more iron, and many women are advised a supplement. It can cause constipation. Water and fibre help.
t1: Iron often makes nausea worse. If it does, ask about taking it at night or starting after 12 weeks.
t2: Most women start a daily iron tablet now. Take it with vitamin C, not with tea, milk or calcium.
t3: Keep taking it. The blood test around 28 weeks tells your doctor whether the dose needs changing.

name: Calcium Supplements
short: Yes. Calcium is commonly recommended in pregnancy. Follow your doctor's advice.
why: It builds your baby's bones and teeth and protects your own stores. It's usually taken at a different time of day from iron, because the two compete to be absorbed.
t1: Not usually needed yet. Food like milk, curd, ragi and sesame covers it. If your doctor prescribes it, take it apart from iron.
t2: Often started now, as your baby's bones build. Take it two hours apart from your iron tablet.
t3: Keep taking it. It also helps with the leg cramps that are common now.

name: Vitamin D
short: Yes. Vitamin D is commonly recommended. Take the dose your doctor sets.
why: It helps your body absorb calcium and keeps bones healthy, yours and your baby's. Many people are a little low in it, so it's often prescribed.

name: Flight Travel
short: Flying is usually fine in an uncomplicated pregnancy. The second trimester is often the most comfortable time.
why: Flying doesn't harm a low-risk pregnancy. On long flights, walk and stretch, drink water, and wear your seatbelt low under your bump. Always check with your doctor before you travel. Later in pregnancy, Indian airlines ask for a letter from your doctor saying you're fit to fly. Each airline sets its own rules on how recent the letter must be and the last week you can fly, so check when you book.
t1: Flying is safe once the pregnancy is settled. If you're bleeding or in pain, or have had a threatened miscarriage, ask your doctor before you book.
t2: Usually the easiest time to travel. Nausea has settled and your bump is still easy to manage.
t3: Many airlines don't allow travel after about 36 weeks and may ask for a doctor's note. Check before you book.

name: Long Road / Train Travel
short: Usually fine. Stop often to move, stretch and use the toilet.
why: Sitting for hours can make your legs swell and feel stiff. Stop every couple of hours, walk a little, drink water, and keep the seatbelt below your bump. Avoid very bumpy roads late in pregnancy.
t1: Fine if you feel up to it. Stop every two hours, and carry snacks for the nausea.
t2: The easiest trimester to travel in. Stop to stretch and walk every two hours.
t3: Stay within reach of your hospital in the last month. Carry your file and your doctor's number.
indian: On a train, book a lower berth and walk the corridor now and then. Carry your pregnancy file, your scan reports, water and snacks. If you're going to your mother's place for the birth, travel before the last month, and meet a doctor there early so they know your history.

name: Yoga
short: Yes. Gentle pregnancy yoga is lovely. Avoid intense poses, deep twists and lying flat on your back later on.
why: Yoga helps flexibility, breathing and calm, and can ease back pain. Choose a pregnancy class or teacher, skip strong tummy and twisting poses, and never push into discomfort.
t1: Gentle pregnancy yoga is fine. Skip hot yoga, deep twists and anything that strains your belly.
t2: The best time for it. Pregnancy classes only, and no long holds lying flat on your back.
t3: Slower and shorter. No upside-down poses, no lying flat on your back, and stop at any dizziness or tightening.

name: Swimming
short: Yes. Swimming is one of the best exercises in pregnancy.
why: The water takes the weight off your joints and back while it works your whole body gently. Avoid diving, very hot pools and slippery edges.
t1: Fine, and gentle when you feel sick and tired. Choose a clean pool.
t2: One of the best exercises now. The water takes the weight off your back.
t3: Still good, as long as your waters haven't broken. Once they break, no pools.

name: Walking
short: Yes. Walking is safe and encouraged all through pregnancy.
why: It's gentle cardio that helps your mood, sleep, digestion and stamina for labour, with almost no downside. Comfortable shoes and a steady pace are all you need.
t3: Keep walking, shorter and slower. It helps your baby settle head-down and eases last-month stiffness.

name: Hair Colour / Dye
short: Usually low-risk, especially from the second trimester. Many women choose ammonia-free dyes or highlights.
why: Very little dye is absorbed through your scalp, so the risk is considered small. To be extra careful, some women wait until after the first trimester, choose gentler formulas and keep the room airy.
t1: Many women wait until after the first trimester, just for peace of mind.
t2: Fine in an airy room. Highlights and ammonia-free colours keep the dye off your scalp.
t3: Fine, with the same care. Skip it if the smell makes you sick.
indian: Natural henna (mehndi) is a popular, gentler way to colour your hair. Patch-test it first, and avoid 'black henna', which can contain harsh chemicals.

name: Waxing
short: Yes. Waxing is generally fine. Your skin may just be more sensitive now.
why: It does your baby no harm. Hormones can make your skin more sensitive and quick to redden, so patch-test new products and tell your salon you're pregnant.
t3: Your skin is more sensitive now and it's hard to see past your bump, so a salon is easier than doing it yourself.

name: Nail Polish
short: Yes. Painting your nails now and then is fine. Just do it in an airy room.
why: The exposure from painting your nails is tiny. Keep a window open or a fan on so you're not breathing in the fumes, and that's all you need.

name: Sex During Pregnancy
short: Yes. Sex is safe in a normal, uncomplicated pregnancy.
why: Your baby is well protected by your womb and the fluid around them, so sex won't hurt them. What feels comfortable changes as your bump grows, so change positions as you need to. If your doctor has asked you to avoid sex, follow that for your pregnancy.
t1: Safe unless your doctor has said otherwise. Bleeding, a low placenta or a past miscarriage are the usual reasons to pause.
t2: Safe, and often more comfortable than early or late pregnancy. Any position that feels right is right.
t3: Safe until your waters break, unless you've been told otherwise. Lying on your sides is easiest. A little spotting afterwards is common. Bleeding is not, so tell your doctor.
indian: It's a very common worry, but sex is a normal, healthy part of pregnancy. Your doctor may advise against it only in specific situations, such as bleeding or placenta previa.

name: Sleeping On Your Back
short: Fine early on. From the second trimester, sleeping on your side (ideally the left) is usually advised.
why: As your womb gets heavier, lying flat on your back can press on a large vein and make you feel dizzy. Sleeping on your side keeps blood flowing well to you and your baby.
t1: Sleep however you're comfortable. There's no restriction yet.
t2: A good time to get used to sleeping on your side. Tuck a pillow behind your back and one between your knees.
t3: The left side is best. If you wake up on your back, just turn over. There's no need to panic.

name: Mosquito Repellent
short: Yes, use it. Mosquito-borne illness is the bigger risk. Choose gentler options and keep the room airy.
why: Dengue, malaria and chikungunya are risky in pregnancy, so protection matters. Creams and roll-ons used as directed are considered fine. Air out the room if you use liquid vaporisers or coils.
indian: This matters most in the monsoon. Creams, patches and nets are better than breathing coil or All Out fumes in a closed room.

name: Dental Treatment
short: Yes. Routine dental care is safe and important. Just tell your dentist you're pregnant.
why: Pregnancy hormones often make gums tender and quick to bleed, so cleanings and needed treatment matter. Vomiting and heartburn bring acid into your mouth, which wears your enamel, so rinse with water afterwards and wait a while before you brush. Most procedures are fine, and dental X-rays use a shield and a tiny, focused dose. Cosmetic whitening can wait until after the birth.
t1: Cleaning and fillings are fine. Tell your dentist you're pregnant. Work you're choosing, not needing, can wait.
t2: The most comfortable time for any planned dental work.
t3: Routine care is fine. Lying flat for a long time is uncomfortable, so ask for a shorter appointment or to be propped up.

name: X-Ray
short: Avoid routine X-rays. If one is medically needed, your doctor will shield you and keep it to a minimum.
why: Imaging that can wait is usually put off until after pregnancy. When an X-ray is needed, say after an injury, the dose is small and your belly is shielded. Always tell the team you're pregnant.
t1: A dental or limb X-ray with a lead apron is a tiny dose. Tell the radiographer you're pregnant. Belly X-rays and CT scans are your doctor's call.
t2: Same: shielded X-rays away from your belly are fine when needed. Ask, and mention the pregnancy.
t3: Same rule to the end. If a belly X-ray is suggested, ask whether an ultrasound could answer the question instead.

name: Sauna / Hot Tub
short: Best avoided. Getting overheated isn't recommended in pregnancy.
why: Saunas, steam rooms and hot tubs can raise your body temperature too much, especially early on. A warm (not hot) bath or shower is the comfortable, safe choice.
t1: This is the trimester to be strictest, because overheating in the first weeks is the concern. No saunas or hot tubs.
t2: Still avoid. A warm bath is fine. A sauna isn't.
t3: Still avoid.

name: Lifting Heavy Things
short: Light lifting is fine. Avoid straining and very heavy loads.
why: Pregnancy hormones loosen your ligaments and your balance shifts, so heavy or awkward lifting puts your back at more risk than your baby. Bend at the knees, hold things close and ask for help with heavy things.
t1: Ordinary loads are fine. Let any strain you feel be your guide. Bend at the knees.
t2: Keep it below what you could lift easily before. Ask for help with heavy things.
t3: Take extra care now. Your centre of gravity is well forward, so it's easier to strain.

name: Fasting
short: Talk to your doctor before you fast. Whether it's okay depends on your health and your stage.
why: Steady food and fluids matter a lot in pregnancy. Some short or partial fasts may be okay for some women. Long or strict fasts are often advised against. It's very individual.
t1: If your nausea is bad, fasting can tip you into dehydration and ketones. Most doctors advise against it now.
t2: A healthy woman usually manages short fasts where fluids are allowed. Ask first, and break the fast if you feel faint.
t3: Not advised. Your baby's needs and your fluid needs are highest now.
indian: For festival vrats, many women keep a fruit-and-milk (phalahar) fast instead of a nirjala one. Please check with your doctor first.

name: Apple
short: Yes. Apples are a great everyday fruit in pregnancy.
why: Good fibre and vitamins that help digestion and energy. Wash them well before eating.

name: Orange / Citrus
short: Yes. Oranges and other citrus fruits are a healthy choice.
why: They're full of vitamin C and water, which help your immunity and keep you hydrated.

name: Grapes
short: Yes, in moderation. Wash grapes well first.
why: A good source of vitamins. Rinse them well and keep portions modest, as they're high in natural sugar.

name: Watermelon
short: Yes. Watermelon is safe and keeps you hydrated.
why: It's mostly water with useful minerals, and great in the heat. Cut it fresh at home instead of buying it pre-cut outside.

name: Muskmelon
short: Yes. Muskmelon is a safe, hydrating fruit.
why: Light and full of water. Wash the rind and cut it fresh at home.

name: Guava
short: Yes. Guava is a nourishing, high-fibre fruit.
why: Rich in fibre and vitamin C, and it helps with constipation. Wash it well.

name: Pomegranate
short: Yes. Pomegranate is a healthy choice in pregnancy.
why: Full of nutrients that support your iron, and antioxidants. A gentle, nourishing fruit.

name: Chikoo (Sapota)
short: Yes, in moderation. Chikoo is fine.
why: Sweet and full of energy. Enjoy it in small amounts, as it's high in natural sugar.

name: Custard Apple
short: Yes, in moderation. Custard apple is fine.
why: Nourishing and full of energy. Keep portions small because it's so sweet.

name: Litchi
short: Yes, in small amounts. Litchi is fine.
why: Refreshing and sweet. Eat ripe ones in moderation, and not on an empty stomach.

name: Jackfruit
short: Yes, in moderation. Ripe jackfruit is fine.
why: Enjoy ripe jackfruit in small amounts. There's no good reason to fear it in normal quantities.

name: Dates
short: Yes. Dates are a lovely pregnancy snack.
why: Rich in iron and natural energy, and often suggested later in pregnancy. Enjoy a few a day.
t1: Fine as a snack, two or three a day. They're dense in sugar.
t2: Fine. A good snack for iron and fibre.
t3: The one fruit with some evidence behind it: a few dates a day from 36 weeks may help your cervix get ready. Six a day is the amount studied.

name: Figs
short: Yes. Figs are nourishing and safe.
why: Good for fibre, calcium and iron, and they help digestion. Fresh figs or soaked dried ones both work.

name: Berries
short: Yes. Strawberries and other berries are a healthy choice.
why: Rich in vitamin C and antioxidants. Wash them well before eating.

name: Kiwi
short: Yes. Kiwi is a safe fruit, full of vitamins.
why: High in vitamin C and fibre, and gentle on digestion.

name: Pear
short: Yes. Pears are a safe, gentle fruit.
why: Good fibre and water, and easy on the stomach. Wash them well.

name: Dry Fruits & Nuts
short: Yes. Dry fruits and nuts are a great snack.
why: Packed with energy, iron and good fats. Keep portions sensible.

name: Almonds
short: Yes. Almonds are a healthy daily snack.
why: Good fats, protein and vitamin E. A handful a day is lovely, and soaked almonds are easy to digest.

name: Walnuts
short: Yes. Walnuts are nourishing in pregnancy.
why: A good source of omega-3 fats that support your baby's development. A few a day is plenty.

name: Cashews
short: Yes, in moderation. Cashews are fine.
why: Tasty and nourishing. Keep to a small handful, as they're high in calories.

name: Peanuts
short: Yes. Peanuts are safe unless you're allergic.
why: A good plant protein. Avoid them only if you have a known peanut allergy.

name: Makhana
short: Yes. Makhana (fox nuts) is a great light snack.
why: Low in fat, and lovely roasted for a light nibble.

name: Sabudana
short: Yes. Sabudana is safe and easy to digest.
why: A gentle source of energy, popular during fasts. Cook it well.

name: Spinach & Greens
short: Yes. Spinach and leafy greens are excellent.
why: Rich in iron and folate. Wash them very well and cook them. Great for pregnancy.

name: Drumstick (Moringa)
short: Yes, cooked and in moderation. Drumstick is fine.
why: Nourishing in cooked dishes like sambar. Enjoy it in normal food amounts.

name: Brinjal
short: Yes. Brinjal is safe, cooked well.
why: An everyday vegetable. Cook it properly. There's no need to avoid it.

name: Potato
short: Yes. Potato is safe in pregnancy.
why: A staple carbohydrate. Balance it with vegetables and protein.

name: Tomato
short: Yes. Tomatoes are safe and healthy.
why: Rich in vitamins. Wash them well. Fine raw in salads made at home, or cooked.

name: Carrot
short: Yes. Carrots are a healthy, safe vegetable.
why: Good for vitamin A and fibre. Wash and peel them before eating raw.

name: Beetroot
short: Yes. Beetroot is safe and nourishing.
why: It supports your iron levels and adds natural colour. Wash it well.

name: Sprouts
short: Sprouts are best eaten cooked, not raw.
why: Raw sprouts can carry bacteria. Steaming or cooking them lightly makes them much safer.
t1: Cooked sprouts are fine. Raw sprouts carry a risk of listeria and salmonella, and the first trimester is the worst time for an infection.

name: Raw Salad
short: Salads are healthy if they're washed very well.
why: Raw vegetables are good for you, but wash them well in clean water. Salads from outside are the main risk.
t1: Washed at home, they're fine. Restaurant salads are the risk (listeria, and unwashed leaves).

name: Mushroom
short: Yes. Cooked mushrooms are safe.
why: Common edible mushrooms are fine when cooked well. Avoid wild or unfamiliar ones.

name: Egg
short: Yes. Well-cooked eggs are a great protein.
why: Cook until both the white and the yolk are firm. Avoid runny or raw eggs.
t1: Well cooked, with no runny yolk. A good protein when little else appeals.

name: Chicken
short: Yes. Well-cooked chicken is safe and nourishing.
why: A good protein. Cook it right through until no pink is left.

name: Mutton
short: Yes, in moderation. Well-cooked mutton is fine.
why: A good source of iron. Cook it through and keep portions reasonable, as it's heavy.

name: Fish
short: Most cooked fish is healthy. Limit the high-mercury kinds.
why: Low-mercury fish like rohu are good for your baby's development. Limit large fish such as king mackerel and shark.
t1: Cooked fish is a good food now. Choose small fish (rohu, pomfret, sardines) and avoid the big predators (shark, swordfish, king mackerel).
t2: Two servings a week of cooked, low-mercury fish is ideal for your baby's brain.
t3: Same. Well cooked, never raw or smoked.

name: Prawns
short: Yes. Well-cooked prawns are safe.
why: Fully cooked prawns and shrimp are fine. Avoid raw or undercooked seafood.

name: High-Mercury Fish
short: Large high-mercury fish are best avoided.
why: Shark, swordfish and king mackerel can be high in mercury, so choose smaller fish instead. If you've already had some, one meal is unlikely to be a problem. Switch to smaller fish from now on.

name: Dal & Lentils
short: Yes. Dal and lentils are excellent in pregnancy.
why: A staple plant protein with fibre and iron. Eat as much as you like.

name: Soya
short: Yes, in moderation. Soya is fine.
why: A useful protein in tofu, soya chunks or soya milk. Keep to normal food amounts.

name: Rajma & Chana
short: Yes. Rajma and chana are healthy, protein-rich foods.
why: Beans and chickpeas give you protein, fibre and iron. Soak and cook them well.

name: Milk
short: Yes. Pasteurised milk is great in pregnancy.
why: A good source of calcium and protein. Choose pasteurised or boiled milk.

name: Cheese
short: Hard and pasteurised cheeses are fine. Avoid soft unpasteurised ones.
why: Cheddar and processed cheese are safe. Avoid mould-ripened or unpasteurised soft cheeses.
t1: Hard cheeses and processed cheese are fine. Soft, mould-ripened cheeses (brie, camembert) and unpasteurised ones carry the listeria risk.

name: Ghee & Butter
short: Yes, in normal amounts. Ghee and butter are fine.
why: Everyday cooking fats, fine in your food. Keep the quantity sensible.

name: Mithai (Mawa Sweets)
short: Mithai made from pasteurised mawa is fine, in moderation.
why: Khoya sweets are fine now and then if they're fresh and clean. The worries are adulteration, freshness and sugar.
t3: For many women, festival season and the last trimester overlap. If your sugars are being watched, have one piece, not the box.

name: Oats
short: Yes. Oats are a lovely pregnancy breakfast.
why: High in fibre, they help digestion and keep you full. Have them with milk and fruit.

name: Poha
short: Yes. Poha is a light, safe meal.
why: Easy to digest, and it can be made rich in iron. A gentle everyday option.

name: Instant Noodles
short: Instant noodles are fine as an occasional treat.
why: Low in nutrition and high in salt. Have them once in a while, ideally with added vegetables and an egg.

name: Fried Snacks
short: Samosa, pakora and the like are fine now and then.
why: Tasty but oily. Enjoy them occasionally, ideally freshly made and clean.

name: Maida (Refined Flour)
short: Yes, in moderation. Foods made with maida are fine.
why: Refined flour has little fibre. Balance it with whole grains and vegetables.

name: Pickle (Achar)
short: Yes, in small amounts. Pickle is fine.
why: It adds flavour but is very high in salt and oil. A little is okay.
t1: Craving achar is very common. A spoonful is fine. The salt is what to watch.
t3: If you've been told to watch your blood pressure or swelling, achar is one of the biggest sources of salt on your plate.

name: Saffron (Kesar)
short: Yes. A few strands of saffron are fine.
why: Saffron in milk, in tiny cooking amounts, is fine. There's no need for large quantities.
t1: A pinch in milk is a tradition. In the first trimester most doctors say a small pinch and no more, because large amounts stimulate the uterus.
t2: A pinch in milk at bedtime is fine. The belief that it makes a baby fair has no basis, but the relaxation is real.
t3: A pinch is fine. Don't take it as a supplement in larger amounts.

name: Turmeric / Haldi Doodh
short: Yes. Haldi doodh in normal amounts is comforting and safe.
why: Turmeric in cooking and a cup of haldi milk are fine. Avoid very large supplement doses.

name: Jaggery (Gud)
short: Yes, in moderation. Jaggery is a fine natural sweetener.
why: It's often chosen over white sugar and may help your iron a little. It's still sugar, so keep it moderate.

name: Spices & Herbs
short: Yes. Everyday cooking spices and herbs are safe.
why: Normal cooking amounts of jeera, dhania, ajwain, hing and garlic are fine. Only very large medicinal doses are worth avoiding.

name: Salt
short: Use normal amounts of salt, and avoid too much.
why: You need some salt, but a lot can worsen swelling and blood pressure. Use iodised salt.
t3: If your blood pressure is being watched, salt is the one thing on the table to cut: pickle, papad, packaged snacks.

name: Sugar
short: Yes, in moderation. Sugar is fine.
why: Enjoy sweet things in small amounts. Too much adds empty calories and affects your blood sugar.
t2: A glucose tolerance test is usually done between 24 and 28 weeks. Don't cut sugar in the days before to pass it. It needs a true reading.
t3: If you have gestational diabetes, your dietitian's plan comes before anything on this page.

name: Sushi (Raw Fish)
short: Raw-fish sushi is best avoided.
why: Raw seafood can carry bacteria and parasites. Cooked or vegetarian sushi is a safer choice. If you've already had some, it's rarely a problem. Tell your doctor if you get a fever, vomiting or diarrhoea.

name: Raw / Undercooked Meat
short: Avoid raw or undercooked meat.
why: It can carry infections like toxoplasma, so always cook meat right through. If you've already eaten some, most of the time nothing comes of it. Tell your doctor if you get a fever or flu-like aches in the weeks after.

name: Cold Cuts / Deli Meat
short: Heat cold cuts until they're steaming hot before you eat them.
why: Ready-to-eat cold meats can carry listeria. Heating them right through makes them safer.
t1: Avoid cold cuts unless they're heated until steaming, because of listeria.

name: Leftover Food
short: Leftovers are fine if they're stored and reheated properly.
why: Put them in the fridge soon and reheat until piping hot. Avoid food that's been left out for long.
t1: Reheat until steaming hot, and eat within a day. The nausea months are a bad time for a stomach infection.

name: Spicy Food
short: Yes. Spicy food is fine if it agrees with you.
why: It won't harm your baby. It may worsen heartburn for some women, so go by what feels comfortable.

name: Chyawanprash
short: Chyawanprash is generally fine in a small daily amount.
why: A traditional tonic that's usually okay. Check with your doctor if you're unsure about the ingredients.
t1: It has many herbs and sugar. Skip it in the first trimester unless an Ayurvedic doctor and your obstetrician both agree.

name: Milkshake
short: Yes. A homemade milkshake is a nice, safe treat.
why: Made with pasteurised milk and fruit, it's nourishing. Go easy on added sugar.

name: Fresh Juice
short: Yes. Juice made fresh at home is fine.
why: Drink it fresh and cleanly made. Whole fruit is even better, for the fibre.

name: Packaged Juice
short: Packaged juice is okay now and then.
why: It's high in sugar and low in fibre. Fresh fruit or fresh juice is better.

name: Lemon Water
short: Yes. Lemon water is safe and refreshing.
why: It keeps you hydrated and can ease nausea. A lovely everyday drink.

name: Sugarcane Juice
short: Sugarcane juice is fine if it's fresh and clean.
why: Refreshing and full of energy. The worry is roadside hygiene, so choose a clean, fresh source.
t1: Only from a stall you trust, with a machine that looks clean. The hygiene is the issue, not the cane.
t2: Same hygiene rule. If a glucose test is due, it's a big sugar load the day before.
t3: If you have gestational diabetes, skip this one. A glass is a lot of sugar at once.

name: Lassi
short: Yes. Lassi made from fresh curd is safe and cooling.
why: A probiotic, calcium-rich drink, sweet or salted, made cleanly.

name: Energy Drinks
short: Energy drinks are best avoided.
why: They're high in caffeine and stimulants that aren't recommended in pregnancy. If you've had one, it's unlikely to be a problem. Switch to water, lemon water or coconut water from now on.
t1: Avoid them. The caffeine in one can alone can go over the daily limit.

name: Herbal Tea
short: Check each herbal tea before you drink it.
why: Some herbs aren't advised in pregnancy. Ginger and other mild teas are usually fine, but check the blend.

name: Smoothie
short: Yes. Homemade fruit smoothies are nourishing.
why: A great way to get fruit, curd and nuts. Make them fresh and clean.

name: Kombucha
short: Kombucha is best avoided in pregnancy.
why: It's fermented, sometimes unpasteurised and slightly alcoholic, so it's safer to skip. If you've had a glass, it's rarely a problem. Leave it for now.
t1: Avoid it: it's unpasteurised and contains a little alcohol.

name: Diet Soda
short: Diet soda is okay now and then.
why: Artificial sweeteners are generally considered fine in small amounts, but these drinks add little.

name: Aam Panna
short: Yes. Aam panna is a safe, cooling summer drink.
why: It keeps you hydrated and helps in the heat. Make it fresh and clean.

name: Badam Milk
short: Yes. Badam milk is a nourishing, safe drink.
why: Milk with almonds gives you calcium and good fats. Lovely warm or cold.

name: Decaf Coffee
short: Yes. Decaf coffee is a good low-caffeine choice.
why: It has very little caffeine, so it's gentle. A nice swap if you miss your coffee.

name: Jaljeera
short: Yes. Jaljeera is safe and helps digestion.
why: A cumin drink that can settle your stomach. Make it cleanly.

name: ORS / Electrolytes
short: Yes. ORS and electrolyte drinks help when you're dehydrated.
why: Useful in the heat, with vomiting or when you feel weak. Use standard ORS as directed.

name: Aspirin
short: Take aspirin only if your doctor prescribes it.
why: Low-dose aspirin is sometimes prescribed in pregnancy, but never start it yourself.
t1: Never on your own. A low dose is prescribed to some women from 12 weeks to lower the risk of pre-eclampsia. That's your doctor's decision.
t2: If you were started on low-dose aspirin, keep taking it as prescribed. Don't add regular aspirin for pain.
t3: Your doctor will tell you when to stop the low dose, usually around 36 weeks. Never full-dose aspirin.

name: Antihistamines (Cetirizine)
short: Ask your doctor before taking allergy medicines.
why: Some antihistamines are used in pregnancy, but check the choice and the dose with your doctor.
t1: Most doctors prefer to avoid anything that isn't essential in the first twelve weeks. If your allergies are bad, ask which antihistamine they prefer.
t2: Cetirizine and loratadine are the ones usually chosen when needed, if your doctor agrees.
t3: Same. Ask before any new medicine.

name: Antacids
short: Yes. Most simple antacids are fine for heartburn.
why: Antacids based on calcium or magnesium are commonly used. Follow the label, and ask your doctor if you need them often.
t1: Fine when needed. Heartburn is less common this early, so ask whether your nausea needs its own treatment.
t2: Fine. The calcium-based ones give you a little calcium too. Check the label for aluminium and avoid those.
t3: Heartburn peaks now and antacids help a lot. If you need them all day, every day, ask about a prescription option.

name: Acidity Tablets (Pantoprazole)
short: Acidity tablets like pantoprazole need your doctor's okay.
why: They're sometimes used in pregnancy. Take them on medical advice, not on your own.
t3: Prescribed for severe heartburn when antacids stop working. On prescription, they're fine.

name: Vitamin C
short: Yes. Vitamin C from food, or a prescribed dose, is fine.
why: It helps your immunity and iron absorption. Avoid very high supplement doses unless you're advised to take them.

name: Prenatal Multivitamin
short: Yes. A pregnancy multivitamin is usually recommended.
why: Take a pregnancy-specific multivitamin as advised. Don't stack extra high-dose vitamins on top.

name: Omega-3 (DHA)
short: Yes. Omega-3 (DHA) supplements are commonly recommended.
why: They support your baby's brain and eyes. Take a pregnancy-safe one as advised.
t1: Fine, and useful. Choose a fish-oil capsule purified of mercury, or an algae one.
t2: Your baby's brain grows fastest from now, so this is when DHA matters most.
t3: Keep taking it. Some doctors stop it near your due date, so ask yours.

name: Vitamin B12
short: Yes. Vitamin B12 is fine and often recommended.
why: It's important for you and your baby, especially if you're vegetarian. Take it as advised.

name: Anti-Nausea (Ondansetron)
short: Anti-nausea medicines should be prescribed by your doctor.
why: Medicines like ondansetron are used for severe vomiting, but only on medical advice.
t1: Prescribed for severe nausea when nothing else works. There's a small debate about it in the first trimester, so it's your doctor's call, not the chemist's.

name: Morning-Sickness Tablet (Doxylamine)
short: Doxylamine for morning sickness needs a prescription.
why: A common option doctors prescribe for nausea, often with vitamin B6. Take it as directed.
t1: The usual first prescription for morning sickness, taken at night. Considered safe, on prescription.

name: Cough Syrup
short: Check with your doctor before any cough syrup.
why: Some contain ingredients best avoided in pregnancy. Your doctor can suggest a safe one.
t1: Most syrups have ingredients best avoided. Try honey, warm water and steam first, and ask before buying any syrup.
t2: Same. Some plain syrups are considered fine, and your doctor knows which.
t3: Same.

name: Throat Lozenges
short: Yes. Plain throat lozenges are generally fine.
why: Simple menthol or honey-lemon lozenges are okay for a sore throat. Ask before using medicated ones.

name: Vicks / Balm
short: Yes. Vicks and balms on the skin are generally fine.
why: Rubbed on the skin or used in steam, they're usually okay. Don't swallow them.
t1: Fine on your chest and under your nose. Keep it off broken skin.

name: Laxatives
short: Try food and water first, and ask before taking laxatives.
why: Fibre, water and isabgol help constipation. Stronger laxatives need medical advice.
t1: Isabgol and more water first. Stimulant laxatives aren't the first choice.
t2: Same. Iron tablets are the usual cause, and a different brand can help.
t3: Same. Ask for a stool softener if the gentle options aren't enough.

name: Isabgol (Psyllium)
short: Yes. Isabgol is a safe option for constipation.
why: A gentle fibre that eases constipation. Take it with plenty of water.
t2: Fine, with a full glass of water. Constipation from iron tablets is common now.
t3: Fine. It's the gentlest option for late-pregnancy constipation.

name: Probiotics
short: Yes. Probiotics are generally considered safe.
why: Curd and probiotic supplements can help digestion. Choose a trusted brand.
t1: Curd is the easiest probiotic. Capsules are fine if you prefer them.

name: Ashwagandha
short: Ashwagandha is best avoided in pregnancy.
why: This herb is traditionally not advised in pregnancy. Skip it unless your doctor says otherwise.
t1: Avoid it. It's traditionally not given in pregnancy and there's no safety data. This is the trimester it matters most.
t2: Avoid.
t3: Avoid.

name: Ayurvedic / Herbal Medicine
short: Check any Ayurvedic or herbal medicine with your doctor.
why: Natural doesn't always mean safe in pregnancy, and product quality varies. Check first.

name: Homeopathy
short: Talk to your doctor about any homeopathic remedy.
why: If you use homeopathy, let your doctor know. Don't stop prescribed medicines for it.

name: Sleeping Pills
short: Avoid sleeping pills unless they're prescribed.
why: Most sedatives aren't recommended. Talk to your doctor about safe ways to sleep better.
t1: Avoid them. The nausea and worry that steal your sleep have safer fixes. Ask before taking anything.
t3: Sleeplessness late in pregnancy is normal. A pillow between your knees and a lighter evening meal work better than any tablet. Ask before taking anything.

name: Diclofenac / Nimesulide
short: These painkillers are generally avoided in pregnancy.
why: They're anti-inflammatories that usually aren't advised, especially later on. Paracetamol is preferred.
t1: Avoid them. Take paracetamol instead.
t2: Avoid them unless your doctor prescribes them for a specific reason.
t3: Avoid them completely in the last trimester.

name: Antifungal / Antiseptic Cream
short: Check skin creams like antifungals with your doctor.
why: Many creams are used on the skin in pregnancy, but check that the one you have is suitable.
t1: Creams for thrush and fungal patches are generally fine on the skin. Tablets are not. Ask which cream.

name: Deworming Tablet
short: Deworming should be timed and approved by your doctor.
why: Some deworming medicines are put off in pregnancy. Let your doctor decide the timing.
t1: Not in the first trimester unless your doctor specifically prescribes it.
t2: Where worms are common, the national programme gives a single dose of albendazole after the first trimester. Your doctor decides.
t3: Same. Only if prescribed.

name: Thyroid Medicine
short: Yes. Keep taking your thyroid medicine as prescribed.
why: Thyroid tablets are important and usually continued in pregnancy. Your doctor will adjust the dose.
t1: Never stop it. Your baby depends on your thyroid hormone in the first weeks. Most women need a higher dose now, so get your level checked as soon as you know you're pregnant.
t2: Keep taking it. Levels are usually checked each trimester.
t3: Keep taking it. The dose often goes back to your pre-pregnancy dose after birth.

name: Blood Pressure Medicine
short: Never stop or change your BP medicine on your own.
why: Some BP medicines are switched in pregnancy. Your doctor will choose a safe one and adjust it.
t1: Some blood pressure medicines are switched for pregnancy-safe ones, so tell your doctor as soon as you know you're pregnant. Never stop on your own.
t2: Keep taking what was prescribed. Your blood pressure is checked at every visit.
t3: Same. Report headaches, changes in your vision or sudden swelling the same day.

name: Insulin
short: Yes. Insulin is safe and often used in pregnancy.
why: It doesn't cross to your baby and is the usual treatment when needed. Take it as prescribed.
t1: Insulin is the standard, safe treatment for diabetes in pregnancy. Doses often need adjusting from the first weeks.
t2: Needs usually rise through the second trimester. Your doctor adjusts the dose.
t3: Needs rise most now, then drop sharply after birth.

name: Vaccines (TT / Flu / COVID)
short: Yes. The vaccines offered in pregnancy are safe for you and your baby, and they protect you both.
why: Tetanus (TT/Tdap), flu and COVID vaccination are advised in pregnancy. In India, most women get two doses of the tetanus vaccine (now usually Td, which adds diphtheria), four weeks apart, or one booster if they had both doses in a pregnancy in the last three years. The flu vaccine is safe in any trimester, so ask about it at your next visit. The protection from the flu and whooping cough vaccines also passes to your baby for the first months. Your doctor sets your schedule.
t1: The flu vaccine is recommended in any trimester. Live vaccines (MMR, chickenpox) aren't given in pregnancy.
t2: The flu vaccine at any time. The Tdap (whooping cough) shot is given between 27 and 36 weeks, and TT as your doctor schedules it.
t3: Tdap now if you haven't had it yet, so your baby is born with some protection against whooping cough.

name: Driving
short: Yes. Driving is fine as long as you're comfortable.
why: Safe in an uncomplicated pregnancy. Keep the seatbelt low under your bump and take breaks on long drives.
t1: Fine, with the belt low under your bump.
t2: Fine. The lap belt goes under your bump and the shoulder belt between your breasts.
t3: Fine until it's hard to reach the wheel comfortably. Many women stop in the last month. If you're in any accident, however small, get checked.

name: Cycling
short: Gentle cycling is okay early on if you're used to it.
why: Your balance changes as your bump grows, so many women switch to a stationary bike later. Avoid busy traffic and falls.
t1: A stationary bike is safer than the road at every stage. On the road, only if you were a confident rider before.
t2: Your balance starts to change as your bump grows. A stationary bike carries no risk of a fall.
t3: Stationary only. A fall this late lands on your bump.

name: Running / Jogging
short: Light running is okay if you already run. Listen to your body.
why: Carry on gently if you're used to it. Stop if you feel pain, dizziness or pressure, and drink plenty of water.
t1: If you ran before pregnancy, you can usually carry on at an easier pace. Don't start now.
t2: Ease your pace and distance. Your ligaments loosen and your joints are less stable.
t3: Most runners switch to walking now. Your balance shifts and your bump changes your stride.

name: Dancing
short: Yes. Gentle dancing is a joyful, safe way to move.
why: Light dancing is great. Avoid jumps, spins and falls, especially later on.
t1: Fine at an easy pace. Skip jumps and spins if you feel dizzy.
t2: Fine, and the best trimester for it. No jumping, no lifts.
t3: Slow dancing is fine. Anything with jumps or spins is not.

name: Household Chores
short: Yes. Normal housework is fine. Just avoid strain.
why: Everyday chores are good light activity. Avoid heavy lifting, strong chemicals and standing on stools.
t1: Fine. Your tiredness is the limit, not the work.
t2: Fine. Avoid climbing up to high shelves.
t3: Fine, in short stretches. Skip mopping on your hands and knees if it strains your back, and no ladders.

name: Climbing Stairs
short: Yes. Climbing stairs is safe. Just go steadily.
why: Use the railing and take your time. There's no need to avoid stairs in a normal pregnancy.
t3: Fine, but hold the rail. Your balance changes in the last weeks and a fall matters more.

name: Standing Long Hours
short: Standing for long is okay, but take regular breaks.
why: Standing for hours can cause swelling and backache. Sit, move and put your feet up when you can.
t2: Shift your weight and sit when you can. Standing still for hours pools blood in your legs.
t3: Long standing brings swelling and can raise blood pressure. Sit with your feet up every hour if you can.

name: Amusement Rides
short: Skip roller coasters and jerky rides.
why: Sudden jolts and forces are best avoided. Gentle rides without big drops are a safer choice.
t1: Avoid them. The sudden stops and jolts are the concern at every stage.
t2: Avoid.
t3: Avoid.

name: Trekking / Hiking
short: Easy treks are okay. Avoid high altitude and rough trails.
why: Gentle walks in nature are lovely. Avoid steep, slippery routes, high altitude and getting exhausted.
t1: Easy trails only, at heights you're used to. Skip it if you feel faint or sick.
t2: Gentle, low-altitude trails, with company. Your balance and stamina both change.
t3: Not now. A fall, or being far from help, is the risk.

name: Gym Workouts
short: Keep up gentle gym workouts, with guidance.
why: Light strength and cardio are fine if you're used to them. Avoid heavy weights, lying flat later on, and overheating.
t1: Weights you already lift, but lighter. No new programme and no holding your breath.
t2: Lighter weights, more reps, and no exercises lying flat on your back.
t3: Lighter still, seated where you can, and stop at any dizziness. Squats and pelvic floor work are the useful ones now.

name: Keratin / Straightening
short: Skip keratin and chemical straightening for now.
why: These treatments can contain strong chemicals like formaldehyde, so many women wait until after pregnancy.

name: Facial / Clean-up
short: Yes. A gentle facial is fine. Skip strong treatments.
why: A basic facial is relaxing. Avoid harsh peels, strong actives and electrical treatments unless you've checked first.
t3: Fine. Your skin can be more sensitive and pigmented now, so ask for a gentle routine and skip any peel.

name: Chemical Peel
short: Check chemical peels with your doctor or dermatologist.
why: Mild peels may be okay, but stronger acids are often put off. Check first.

name: Botox / Fillers
short: Botox and fillers are best avoided in pregnancy.
why: They're elective and there's little safety data, so most doctors advise waiting until after the birth.

name: Laser Hair Removal
short: Many women put off laser hair removal.
why: It isn't known to be harmful, but your skin is more sensitive and it can wait, so most women wait.
t1: Most clinics won't treat you in pregnancy, and your skin reacts differently now. Wait.
t2: Same: most clinics wait until after birth. Try waxing or shaving instead.
t3: Same.

name: Pedicure / Manicure
short: Yes. A pedicure or manicure is a lovely, safe treat.
why: Enjoy it. Choose a clean salon with good airflow, and ask for a gentle calf massage instead of strong pressure points.

name: Makeup
short: Yes. Everyday makeup is fine.
why: Normal cosmetics are safe. Take them off before bed, and patch-test new products, as your skin can be more sensitive.

name: Sunscreen
short: Yes. Sunscreen is safe and a good idea.
why: It protects skin that darkens more easily now. Mineral sunscreen (zinc oxide, titanium dioxide) is the gentlest. Some women prefer to limit chemical filters like oxybenzone, which is why the ingredient checker marks those as limit.

name: Retinol Creams
short: Avoid retinol and strong vitamin A creams.
why: Retinoid creams are usually advised against in pregnancy. Switch to gentler skincare. If you used one before you knew you were pregnant, stop now and mention it to your doctor.
t1: Stop as soon as you know you're pregnant. Retinoids are the one skincare ingredient with a clear link to birth defects.
t2: Still avoid.
t3: Still avoid, until you've finished breastfeeding.

name: Perfume / Deodorant
short: Yes. Perfume is fine, though strong scents can set off nausea.
why: It's safe to wear. You may just find heavy fragrances hard to bear early on.

name: Hair Oiling (Champi)
short: Yes. Oiling your hair is safe and soothing.
why: A traditional, relaxing routine. A gentle champi is fine.

name: Tattoo / Piercing
short: Many women put off new tattoos and piercings.
why: The main worries are infection and the unknowns, so most women wait until after pregnancy.
t1: Wait. The concern is infection from the needle, and there's no safety standard for ink in pregnancy. Mehndi (natural henna) is fine.
t2: Same. Even a small risk of infection is worth avoiding now.
t3: Same. Also avoid a lower-back tattoo in the last weeks. Some anaesthetists won't place an epidural through fresh ink.

name: Gel / Acrylic Nails
short: Gel or acrylic nails are okay now and then.
why: Generally low risk. Choose an airy salon, and know that your nails may be checked during labour.

name: Smoking
short: Avoid smoking completely.
why: It cuts the oxygen and nutrients reaching your baby. Stopping at any point helps. Ask for support if you need it.
t1: Stopping now gives your baby the most benefit. Ask your doctor about help to quit.
t2: Stopping at any point still helps.
t3: Stopping even now improves your baby's oxygen for birth.

name: Secondhand Smoke
short: Avoid secondhand smoke as much as you can.
why: Breathing in other people's smoke is also harmful. Ask people not to smoke around you.

name: Vaping
short: Vaping and e-cigarettes are best avoided.
why: They still contain nicotine and other substances that aren't safe for your baby. If you vape to stay off cigarettes, ask your doctor about help to quit.

name: Very Hot Bath
short: Warm baths are lovely. Very hot water isn't advised.
why: Avoid very hot baths that raise your body temperature. Keep the water comfortably warm.
t1: Warm, not hot. If the water makes you flush or feel dizzy, it's too hot. Keep baths short.
t2: A warm bath is fine and eases back pain. Not a scalding one.
t3: Warm baths are fine. Get in and out carefully, and not once your waters have broken.

name: Air Conditioning
short: Yes. Air conditioning is completely fine.
why: Staying cool and comfortable is good for you. Just avoid sitting in a cold draught for long.

name: Incense (Agarbatti)
short: Use agarbatti and dhoop in an airy space.
why: Now and then is fine. Avoid breathing heavy smoke in a closed room for long.
t1: If the smoke makes your nausea worse, open a window or skip it.

name: Strong Cleaning Chemicals
short: Everyday cleaning is fine. Use strong cleaners with care and fresh air.
why: Wear gloves, open the windows and never mix products, especially bleach with toilet cleaners. Switch to milder ones where you can: soap and water, diluted vinegar or baking soda do most jobs. Leave drain openers, oven cleaners and strong sprays to someone else.
t1: If strong smells make you sick, this is a good time to hand the bathroom cleaning to someone else.

name: Paint Fumes
short: Avoid heavy paint fumes, and keep the room airy.
why: Brief exposure is unlikely to harm, but avoid painting jobs and strong solvent fumes in closed rooms.
t1: Leave the painting to someone else in the first trimester. Solvent fumes are the concern while your baby's organs are forming.
t2: Water-based paint in an airy room is fine. Skip oil paints and strippers, and let someone else paint the nursery.
t3: Same, and don't climb ladders.

name: Pesticides / Sprays
short: Avoid pesticides and strong sprays.
why: Stay away while spraying happens, and from treated areas. Choose safer pest control and air the room well.

name: Cats / Litter
short: You can keep your cat. Just avoid the litter box.
why: The concern is toxoplasma from cat poo (faeces), so let someone else clean the litter, and wash your hands well.
t1: Toxoplasmosis is the concern, and it matters most in the first trimester. Let someone else change the litter, or wear gloves and wash your hands.
t2: Same rule. Stroking your cat is fine.
t3: Same.

name: Dogs / Pets
short: Yes. Keeping dogs and other pets is fine.
why: Pets are lovely company. Wash your hands, and keep their vaccinations and hygiene up to date.

name: Gardening
short: Gardening is fine. Wear gloves and wash your hands after.
why: Soil can carry toxoplasma, so wear gloves and wash your hands well afterwards.
t1: Gloves on, and wash your hands after. Soil can carry toxoplasma.
t2: Same, and no heavy digging.
t3: Gloves, no bending for long, and no ladders.

name: Public Transport
short: Yes. Buses, trains and the metro are fine.
why: Travel as usual. Ask for a seat, hold on firmly, and avoid the busiest rush hours if you can.

name: Crowded Places
short: Crowded places are okay. Protect yourself from infections.
why: They do no special harm, but keep your distance in flu season and wash your hands often.
t1: Infections are the concern (flu, rubella, chickenpox in the first trimester). A mask in crowds is sensible.
t3: Crowds are tiring, and a knock to your belly is a real risk. Keep visits short.

name: High Heels
short: Low, steady shoes are safer than high heels.
why: Your balance and posture change in pregnancy. Flats or small heels lower the risk of falls and backache.
t2: Go lower as your balance changes. A fall is the risk, not the shoe.
t3: Flat or nearly flat. Swollen feet and a shifted centre of gravity make it easy to fall in heels.

name: Tight Clothes
short: Choose comfortable, loose clothing.
why: Very tight clothes can feel uncomfortable and slow your circulation. Soft, roomy fits feel better.

name: Massage
short: Gentle massage is fine. Choose a therapist trained in pregnancy massage.
why: It's relaxing for your back and legs. Avoid strong pressure on your belly, and go to someone experienced with pregnancy.
t1: Most therapists won't massage in the first trimester. A gentle back and shoulder rub at home is fine.
t2: Pregnancy massage from a trained therapist, lying on your side, is fine and helps your back.
t3: Lying on your side only, gentle, and no deep pressure on your calves and ankles. A foot massage is fine.

name: Spa / Sauna
short: Enjoy gentle spa treatments, but skip the heat.
why: Relaxing massages and facials are fine. Avoid saunas, steam rooms and hot tubs that overheat you.
t1: Facials and manicures are fine. Skip the steam room, hot tub and sauna.
t2: Same: the treatments are fine, the heat rooms aren't.
t3: Same, lying on your side on the couch.

name: Meditation
short: Yes. Meditation is lovely in pregnancy.
why: It eases stress and helps you sleep and feel close to your baby. Practise as often as you like.

name: Mobile / Microwave
short: Yes. Using your phone and microwave is safe.
why: There's no evidence that everyday phone use or microwaves harm your baby. Just rest your neck and eyes now and then.
t3: Fine at every stage. Late-night scrolling can cost you sleep, but the phone does your baby no harm.

name: Stress
short: Some stress is normal. If it doesn't let up, it's worth easing.
why: Worrying now and then is natural. If you feel anxious all the time, rest, talk to someone and tell your doctor.
t1: Nausea, tiredness and worry feed each other. Resting is part of getting better, not laziness.
t2: For most women these are calmer months. If low mood stays, say so at your visit.
t3: Worry about the birth is normal. A birth class and a plan for the day help more than reassurance alone.

name: Hair Removal Cream
short: Usually fine on your legs and arms. Patch-test first, as your skin reacts more easily now.
why: Very little of the cream gets through your skin, so it isn't thought to harm your baby. The trouble is your skin: pregnancy can make it sensitive, and the smell can set off nausea. Patch-test a small area 24 hours before, follow the timing on the pack, and keep it off the bikini area and any broken or irritated skin.
t1: Fine if the smell doesn't bother you. If it makes you queasy, shaving or threading is easier for now.
t2: Fine, with a patch test first. Use it in an airy room.
t3: Fine, but reaching your legs gets hard. Waxing at a salon, or shaving, is often easier now.
indian: Most women use the creams sold at any chemist. Threading and waxing at the parlour are gentle, familiar options that need no chemicals at all.

name: Milk Bath
short: Yes. A warm milk bath is fine. Keep the water warm, not hot.
why: Milk, oats or a little rose water in a warm bath is gentle on dry, itchy skin. The things to watch are the heat and a slippery tub. Keep the water comfortably warm, get in and out slowly, and skip strong essential oils or heavily perfumed bath bombs.
t1: Warm, not hot, and keep it short. Overheating matters most in these weeks.
t2: Fine, and soothing for itchy skin as your bump stretches.
t3: Fine, with care getting in and out. No baths once your waters have broken.
indian: A little besan or haldi mixed with milk, the old ubtan way, is gentle too. Patch-test anything new, as your skin can react more easily now.

name: Hot Yoga
short: Best skipped. Classes in a heated room can raise your body temperature too far.
why: Hot yoga and Bikram classes are held in rooms heated close to 40°C. Overheating is the concern in pregnancy, especially early on, and it's hard to cool down in that heat. Ordinary pregnancy yoga in a cool, airy room gives you the same stretch and calm.
t1: Avoid it. Overheating in the first weeks is the main concern.
t2: Still avoid. Move to a pregnancy yoga class in a normal room.
t3: Still avoid. Gentle stretches and breathing at home are enough now.

name: Masturbation and Orgasm
short: Yes. Masturbation and orgasm are safe in a normal pregnancy.
why: Your baby is well protected by your womb and the fluid around them. After an orgasm your bump may tighten or feel hard for a little while. That's normal and settles with rest. If your doctor has asked you to avoid sex, for example because of bleeding, a low-lying placenta or a risk of early labour, ask whether that includes orgasm too.
t1: Safe unless your doctor has said otherwise. Your desire may rise or fall in these weeks, and both are normal.
t2: Safe. Some women feel more desire now, as more blood flows to the pelvis.
t3: Safe until your waters break, unless you've been told otherwise. Tightenings after orgasm are common. Call your doctor if they keep coming regularly, or if there's bleeding, leaking fluid or pain.

name: Breastfeeding While Pregnant
short: Yes, usually. Most women can keep feeding an older baby or toddler through an uncomplicated pregnancy.
why: Feeding releases a little oxytocin, which can cause mild tightenings, but in a healthy pregnancy this doesn't bring on early labour. Your doctor may ask you to stop if you've had early labour or a miscarriage before, if you're bleeding, or if your placenta is low. Eat and drink a little more, keep taking your pregnancy tablets, and tell your doctor you're still feeding.
t1: Sore nipples and a drop in milk are common now. Neither means anything is wrong.
t2: Your supply often falls around now, and the milk may taste different. Some toddlers stop on their own. Either way is fine.
t3: Your milk changes to colostrum in these weeks. If tightenings come regularly while you feed, or you have pain or bleeding, stop and call your doctor.
indian: Many women in India are still feeding an older child when the next pregnancy begins, and family may say the milk has turned bad for the child. It hasn't. Whether you carry on, wean slowly or feed both after the birth is your choice, made with your doctor.

name: Cannabis / Bhang
short: No. Cannabis in any form, smoked, eaten or drunk as bhang, is best avoided in pregnancy.
why: Its active substance (THC) crosses the placenta and reaches your baby. It's linked with lower birth weight, and no safe amount is known. CBD oils and gummies haven't been shown to be safe either. If you used some before you knew you were pregnant, stop now and tell your doctor. They hear this often and are there to help, not to judge.
t1: Avoid it. If you used it before you knew, stop now and mention it at your next visit.
t2: Avoid it. If it was helping with nausea, pain or sleep, ask your doctor about safer options.
t3: Avoid it. Tell the team caring for you in labour if you've been using it.
indian: Bhang thandai and bhang pakoras go round at Holi and some weddings. Stick to plain thandai this year, and ask what's in anything you're offered.

name: Home Heartbeat Doppler
short: Best skipped. A home heartbeat monitor can give false comfort when your baby needs checking.
why: These devices are sold online to listen to your baby's heartbeat at home. Without training it's easy to pick up your own pulse or the placenta instead, and hearing a heartbeat doesn't mean all is well. Rely on your baby's movements and your doctor's checks. If your baby's movements slow or change, contact your maternity unit straight away, any time, day or night, even if a home device sounds fine.
t1: Too early to be useful. Even a doctor's Doppler often can't find the heartbeat before about 12 weeks, which can cause needless fear.
t2: Once you feel your baby move, get to know their pattern. That tells you more than any device.
t3: Your baby's movements are the sign to watch. If they slow or change, call straight away.

name: Cold and Blocked Nose
short: Most colds settle on their own in about a week. Start with rest, steam and fluids, and ask before taking any cold tablet.
why: Colds are common in pregnancy and don't harm your baby. What helps: rest, plenty of warm fluids, steam, saline nose drops, and honey in warm water for a sore throat. Paracetamol is fine for aches or a fever. Many cold and flu tablets mix a decongestant with other medicines, so ask your doctor before you buy one. Call your doctor the same day if you have a fever of 38°C or more, trouble breathing, or you're no better after a week.
t1: Decongestant tablets are best avoided in the first trimester. Steam, saline drops and rest come first.
t2: Same care. Ask your doctor which cold medicine they prefer, if you need one.
t3: Same. A blocked nose is common late in pregnancy even without a cold, and a saline spray helps.
indian: Haldi doodh, adrak and tulsi chai, and steam over a bowl of hot water are the usual home remedies, and all are fine. Skip a kadha packed with many herbs unless your doctor agrees.
